title: Chapter 4 — Why The Americans Have Never Been So Eager As The French For General Ideas In Political Matters
paragraphs: I observed in the last chapter that the Americans show a less pronounced taste for general ideas than the French — and this is especially true in political matters. The Americans infuse far more general ideas into their legislation than the English do, and they pay much more attention than the English to adjusting the practice of affairs to theory. But no political bodies in the United States have ever shown so warm an attachment to general ideas as the Constituent Assembly and the Convention in France. At no time has the American people seized on ideas of this kind with the passionate energy of the French people in the eighteenth century, or displayed the same blind confidence in the value and absolute truth of any theory. This difference between the Americans and the French comes from several causes, but principally from the following one. The Americans form a democratic people that has always directed public affairs itself. The French are a democratic people that, for a long time, could only speculate about the best way to conduct them. The social condition of France led that people to form very general ideas about government, while its political constitution prevented it from correcting those ideas by experiment and gradually detecting their inadequacy. In America, the two things constantly balance and correct each other.

At first glance, this may seem to contradict what I said before — that democratic nations derive their love of theory from the excitement of their active life. A closer examination will show that there is nothing contradictory in the proposition. People living in democratic countries eagerly seize on general ideas because they have little leisure, and because these ideas spare them the trouble of studying particulars. This is true — but it applies only to matters that are not the necessary and habitual subjects of their thoughts. Merchants will take up very eagerly, and without much close scrutiny, any general ideas on philosophy, politics, science, or the arts that may be presented to them. But as for ideas relating to commerce, they will not accept them without inquiry, or adopt them without reservation. The same thing applies to statesmen with regard to general ideas in politics. If, then, there is a subject on which a democratic people is especially liable to give itself up, blindly and extravagantly, to general ideas, the best corrective will be to make that subject a part of the daily practical work of that people. The people will then be forced to enter into its details, and the details will teach them the weak points of the theory. This remedy may often be a painful one, but its effect is certain.

So it happens that the democratic institutions that compel every citizen to take a practical part in government moderate that excessive taste for general theories in politics which the principle of equality suggests.
